summary: David DiNardo sits down with Alex Lawson, a carpenter who grew up relying on the food bank in Heron Gate, built Capital Framers into a 17-person company, and is now running for mayor of Ottawa. Lawson explains why he sees politics as an extension of entrepreneurship, how he writes policy by talking to bus drivers, police and outreach workers where policy meets reality, and what he would change on crime, drugs, the vacant unit tax, parking and transit. The conversation also covers how he removed himself as the bottleneck in his business, his abundance-over-scarcity leadership style, and what it is like to become a public figure overnight.
takeaways: Alex Lawson never called himself an entrepreneur; carpentry, then the business, then the mayoral run were each just the next problem he decided he could do something about.
Politics is communication, and business is a series of the right communications, so seek to understand first and remember the taxpayer is your employer, not your customer.
Write policy by getting into the weeds with the people where policy meets reality: bus drivers for transit, police ride-alongs for crime, and street outreach workers for drugs and homelessness.
Ottawa runs on leaking buckets; OC Transpo lost $54 million last year while providing poor service, and pouring more money in before patching the holes will not fix it.
Ottawa has a minimum of 42 police officers on duty citywide, the same number as in 1995 before amalgamation, and Lawson wants to double that to 84 over a four-year term.
Ottawa has six or seven places to get a clean pipe or needle but only two or three recovery beds with a week-long wait, so Lawson wants harm reduction paired with a real pathway to recovery.
Lawson would scrap the vacant unit tax and slash paid parking, arguing that fees, tickets and garbage limits are picking taxpayers' pockets while core services decline.
To stop being the bottleneck, give your team responsibility before they are fully ready and accept lower profit at first, because people have to build the muscle and find their own leadership style.
Alex's sticky note on his first laptop would say: keep going.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: We need an entrepreneur in there, and is that what you are?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: I was a carpenter.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: What do you say to business owners to bring businesses back downtown?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Make it a place where you feel good about raising your family again because-

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: What's in it for you? I've lost complete faith in politicians.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: What do you think I'm doing here? They lost $54 million last year while providing terrible service.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: Did you come from an entrepreneur family? Like, was your parents business owners?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Absolutely not.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: Did you anticipate the publicity?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: But it all goes together. This is a quality of life election.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: I can honestly agree with the fact that it's not working in Ottawa.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: You know, I expected it to be busy.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: If you left a sticky note on your first laptop before you ever got started-

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: If I can plug the website, votealex.ca.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: Builder, not politician.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: That's right.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: First thing I saw on your website was that, and we don't need another politician. We need an entrepreneur in there, and is that what you are? And what brought you from entrepreneur to now politician?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: I mean, I guess so. Yeah, I guess you could put that label entrepreneur on it. It's not something I've ever said like, "I'm an entrepreneur," right? I was a carpenter, and then this was the next step, and that was the next step. And then eventually starting the business was the next step, right?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: And then, you know, as you grow the business, rather than thinking, "I'm a businessman," it was really just, "This is the next thing that I have to do." And, you know, it seems like a big jump from that to politics, but what is an entrepreneur? It's identifying an issue, knowing that you can actually do something about it, and then getting involved, whether it's, you know, in a business for profit or for providing a service that you know is a niche where you're gonna get a market.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: But the reason I got into politics was really just not seeing somebody that I could get behind, not seeing somebody that represented my interests, your interests, the interests of the worker, right? The common taxpayer. I've been a lot of different people, you know, on the entrepreneurial track as you are, right?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: I started out, I grew up in Heron Gate with no stranger to the food bank, getting snowsuits from the snowsuit fund, and now I'm the business owner with 17 guys, three kids. Oldest is off to university now. But between these two people, you're, you know, you're a lot of different people in the city of Ottawa.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: You've walked a lot of different roads wearing a lot of different pairs of shoes, and you understand the friction points that everybody's experiencing, right? You understand better what somebody worries about in their day-to-day, and I think that that's what we need to bring to the mayor's office.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: And when was that click happen? Like, have you been thinking about it for a while, and then you're finally like, "I gotta do it"?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: No, not really. It wasn't-- I mean, you don't make the decision to run for mayor overnight. You know, when it was like, okay, well, maybe I am gonna be that person and be that change that I wanna see.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: But it's not, you know, it's not click at the moment. I was hmming and hawing about it for a couple of months, but before that, I didn't see myself getting involved in politics and being a candidate. You know, I'd see myself more as I'll help somebody out that I see that I believe could represent me at Queen's Park or at Parliament or at City Hall, and help them achieve that goal.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: But I never thought I would be the one. But having that conversation with people again, like, okay, well, who's actually gonna provide the basic services or provide them appropriately? And I voted for Mark Sutcliffe in the last election, right? 'Cause he promised safe, reliable, affordable. Sounded like we were gonna get back to basics and we were gonna pay attention to those things.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: And then instead, while our infrastructure is crumbling under our feet and we got libraries that can't even be open on Sundays, and we've got people literally dying in our streets from drug overdoses and more stabbings and shootings than we've had before, we're focusing on building Lansdowne 2.0, and we're restricting how much garbage people can put out, so it's just led to an increase in dumping.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: We've got a transit service that still doesn't work properly 'cause nobody's, no politician anyway, is bothered to go and actually understand what the problems are here.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: And politician to builder, those are two completely different fields. Even though you've built your business, you've built your family, you've built everything, do you find any correlation around both of those and how to handle different situations or-

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Absolutely.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: I mean, I'd kind of flip that around and get you to define politician. When a lot of people are saying you don't have political experience, well, what is politics if not it's communication? And what is business if not a series of the right communications? I mean, there's putting in the work in both of these things as well, but you're gonna be successful if you seek to understand first and then to be understood, right?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: You have to see things from other people's perspectives, whether it's making sales as an entrepreneur with your business and understanding the customer's needs, or it's understanding the taxpayer's needs. Because at the end, it kind of flips it around because the taxpayer's not your customer, they are your employer.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: But it's understanding what their needs are and being able to actually provide that properly. So, when people say that I don't have any political experience, I mean, I just kind of shrug it off. I don't agree at all.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: And how's the campaign trail been going thus far?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: It's been great. It's been great.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: I think the message is really resonating with people. It's who I am. It's the work that I've been putting in over the last few months has been to understand what's going on. The first thing we did was reach out to a bunch of community associations. I think 20-something of them got back to us out of 120-odd, and having conversations with them.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Not going there to promise them a new speed bump or a slide or a, you know, a water park, but to just say, "What, like, give me a perspective of what's going on in your neighborhood." 'Cause we are a patchwork quilt in Ottawa, right? We're a bunch of rural and suburban and urban core, a lot of different neighborhoods, a lot of different histories there, a lot of different, you know, heritage of the neighborhoods.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: And it's not gonna be a one-sized-fits-all approach that solves everybody's issues. But there are trends that pop up no matter where you are in the city. Things like people just want a safe place to cross the street. Or I've had, you know, with OC Transpo for the transit policy that's up on votealex.ca, we put that out early May.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: There's actually been a few things that the new manager has implemented from that policy. There's still a lot that can be done. But I wrote that by getting down into the weeds with bus drivers. And there was bus drivers calling me eventually, saying, "Alex, I know that you're the one that'll actually hear me out and listen to me, the operator, to see what's going on."

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: If you wanna learn how to bake bread, you talk to a baker. You wanna learn how to build a house, you're gonna talk to a framer. If you wanna know how to make a bus show up on time, talk to the bus driver. And that's the approach that I've been taking to everything, is getting down into the weeds as deep as I can, talking to the people where policy meets reality.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: That's been the same thing for drugs and homelessness, and, you know, so many different areas, and I think that's really resonating with people that they know that I'm not somebody that's just gonna promise a solution from a high level. Like, oh, we have a drug crisis. Let me just sprinkle some money on that, and it'll all go away.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: No. We've got... OC Transpo's a great example. There's so many examples in the city where we've got leaking buckets, and we have politicians promising to pay more, pour more water into these leaking buckets than ever before. I mean, that's not something to be bragging about. I mean, yeah, a lot of things are gonna get wet, but the water's not gonna get where you need it to go.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: We need to patch the holes in those buckets before we start filling them up even more.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: Me being a business owner, I'm thinking, like, whenever I wanna get some stuff done, in the private sector, you get stuff done. You figure it out. You hire people. You can, you know, build a team around you. When you go into politics, there could be already an existing team.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: There could be an already existing infrastructure that's already been built for years. How do you unravel what's been built up for decades and change the homelessness, the crime, all of these different huge items?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Yeah, no, you're right. Starting to unravel that is going to be the biggest challenge, and I think it's where others have not seen so much success.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: As I said, I did vote for the current mayor, right? I did believe in him, and I do still believe that he has good intentions. But I think he came up against a pretty strong established bureaucracy that has been doing things a certain way for the last decade, maybe longer, and it's been difficult to push back against that.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: You have to be willing to have those difficult conversations and to actually get in and have an understanding of it. I mean, I've done ride-alongs with the Ottawa Police Service, and I intend to do, you know, more of a kind of a ride-along thing with bylaw services once I'm in, or with 311, or with the planning department, or with whomever it is to see where the friction points are and talk to the people that are in these departments in the city of Ottawa and actually get to try to have a better understanding and have a look at our managers.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Are some of them, are they there because they were good at their job, or are they there because they knew somebody? That's gonna be probably the biggest challenge. I mean, there is getting a council vote on your side as well. But I think that's one of the main differences between running for councilor and running for mayor as well.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: People often ask me why I didn't start with councilor. Well, I don't see them as the same job at all. I'm not trying to argue for one neighborhood, because the problems in our city are really systematic. They are citywide, and sometimes they're showing up in different ways in different communities.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: But I think it's, as a whole, it is the system and being a different job that, you know, the mayor has more of an impact on the city staff and the bureaucracy. So that's why I think it's a different job, and that's the direction that I went.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: Yeah, I mean, you could see firsthand, like, I have property downtown Ottawa, and I typically never go there anymore.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: I went down a couple months ago, and I couldn't believe after, you know, six months to nine months of not being down there, what I saw going downtown of the, you know, the everything, the atmosphere and everything has completely changed. Like, what do you say to business owners to bring businesses back downtown?

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: And I know you talked a lot about recently back to office and, you know, the government's going back to the office, and you not necessarily agreeing with it. Like, has to work for the individual from the last clip I saw. Like, how do you get businesses back to Ottawa, and how do you get entrepreneurs not to leave Ottawa to go to the States now?

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: Like, there's a fight not only internally, but globally as well to get people to different regions.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Yeah. Well, I mean, I think you just nailed it right there. You have properties down there and you don't wanna go there, right? When there's a business down there, people don't wanna go there.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: And we made sure to put our campaign office right in the heart of one of the areas. In the heart of Somerset Ward. We're at 45 Eccles, right beside the Somerset Community Health Center. And, you know, for a lot of the people volunteering on my campaign, it's scary for them to cross that parking lot to get to the office.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Just this morning, there were people that decided to come out from the road to make a drug deal, like, right under my window. And that's just the reality downtown now, is people don't feel safe. And so it's not gonna be about necessarily forcing everybody back to the office. It, you know, they're not going to be taking part in these businesses.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: They're gonna be... With the amount of time that they're spending traveling, they're gonna be going there, doing their work, and then they're gonna be getting out. Let's make it so that people wanna go there for leisure, right? Let's make sure that people actually feel safe there. Let's make sure that they can actually get there.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: And there's been a lot of business owners in the different areas that have been calling me. There was Pet Circus on Bank Street, Bank and Cooper, and he's like, "Alex, my councilor won't answer me. The BIA that's supposed to be, you know, making sure that the business' best interests are upheld, they don't say anything about this.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: They're just happy to throw us a little live music event and pat themselves on the back with all the money that they take from me and from the city for being a member." They just don't feel represented at all. But he's like, "Look at this. We used to have people come in to see the fish with their families as they walked by.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Maybe they'd buy something, maybe they wouldn't." But he said in the last two years, his sales are down over 50% because people just don't wanna come to that area anymore. There was a property owner on Argyle who's got his first level's commercial, and then the upper floors are condos. All of his tenants wanna break their lease early, and he can't blame them.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: It's terrifying there. There was one of his tenants was getting into her car, and there was somebody there in the parking lot that, you know, not a resident, wasn't supposed to be there, that turned around and actually urinated on her. Like he was taking a piss, turned around and pissed on her.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Like, this is what's actually going on down there. He showed me a video of somebody that was walking his dog, and then somebody came running out of his backyard, or the back parking lot, and tried to stab him with a box cutter, and then you just see the guy running off. And he said that it's not really the...

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: The councilor won't come and see him. The mayor wouldn't come and see him. He's reaching out to the mayor and he's, as I guess he knows him, and he's saying, "Hey, come down and you gotta see what's going on here." And he's like, "Yeah, yeah, I'll send a staff member." The councilor's not listening. The police have been great, he said.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: They do respond within minutes. He can text the officers in the area, and that's what's been great about the community policing model. You get to know them. But, you know, so they're there in four minutes, but it's gonna happen again two hours later. It's gonna happen again two hours later.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: But how do you change all this? Like, talk about stomaching all of this stuff and putting it on your shoulders at the end of the day as a mayor. Like, as a business owner, I put that on my shoulders. If I'm running 20 people or 30 people or 40 people, I need to get the job done, right? You're talking about a big city that has a lot of changes.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Well, you gotta look at, yeah, I think you gotta take a different look at what the job is that you need to be doing, and the approach that the city's been taking right now. And we're just keeping people sick right now. We're a full harm reduction without a pathway to recovery. So, talking about getting down into the details and talking to people where policy meets reality, I've been going out with a couple of outreach groups, Steps Off the Street being one of them, SOS.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: And the guy that's running that, Gerald Jorgensen, he was homeless on the streets in Ottawa, addicted to fentanyl for a couple of years, sleeping rough, sleeping outside, and he managed to get himself clean. And so now he's doing the outreach, not just to make today a little better for somebody 'cause he gives them a jacket when it's cold or a blanket or, you know, a sandwich when they're hungry or water or all these great things that he's doing.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: He's doing it to have the conversation with the person that he probably knew from when he was living out there and say, "Hey, man," like, "you don't actually have to live like this." And, you know, after the second or third time, sometimes somebody's having a rough day and they're like, "Yeah, you know what, Gerald?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: I'm ready." Like, "I don't wanna live like this anymore." But he has to drive them to Kingston to get them into a treatment program because we just don't have nearly enough services in Ottawa. There's a million places, not a million, but I mean, there's probably six or seven places in Ottawa where you can go to get a clean crack pipe or a needle or, you know, a kit to cook your drugs.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: But to actually get into recovery, there's two, maybe three places, and it's gonna be a week-long wait, whereas you can get something to do more drugs right away. So until we change our approach and we start looking at recovery as really the only option, yeah, harm reduction in the meantime so that we can get them to there, but-

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: So you're talking more facilities in Ottawa?

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Yeah, more facilities in Ottawa, and this is gonna be something that we gotta work with the provincial government on. Let's discourage drug use, and let's actually start cracking down on the people that are preying on the vulnerable people. And the vulnerable, I mean the ones that are addicted to drugs.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Let's start busting the drug dealers again. And it's just not a dangerous place to be a drug-- Talk about entrepreneurs, I mean, I don't wanna say it, but, you know, you want an easy, or not an easy job, but you want a job where you can make some money right now in Ottawa, sell drugs. It's not dangerous anymore.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Because right now we have... Do you know what the minimum number of cops on the street in Ottawa is?

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: It's 42 for the entire city. So from past Dunrobin to past Sarsfield, past Osgoode, with over a million people, we have 42 officers on duty minimum at any given time. That's the same number as it was in 1995, before amalgamation.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: So when it was just the city of Ottawa, much smaller, before we took on Kanata and Orleans, before all of the amalgamation, it was 42 officers, and we were half the population. And then the suburbs, what is suburbs now, the other towns, they had police forces or they had OPP. So all that went away, and we still just have a minimum 42 officers on the street.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: So not saying policing is the only strategy. We also have to look at getting people into recovery, 'cause, you know, whose harm are we really reducing when I'm knocking on doors in the Glebe and they're telling me that their kids are counting needles on the way home from school? Or coming home from Glashan, they're counting how many needles they see.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: That's a new game. So one of the things that we're going to do over, you know, over the four-year period, not overnight, is we're gonna double that number. We're gonna make the minimum number of police 84. We need to fund our police department a lot better, and I've done a couple of ride-alongs with them, as I mentioned.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: I've met with the president of the police union. I've met with the police chief. And they can't investigate fraud under $25,000 right now. That's how bad it is. So when an old lady's getting ripped off for 500 bucks in a scam or whatever it is, they can't even look into it. I mean, if your place got robbed tomorrow, call them.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: They're gonna be like, "Yeah, here's your form to fill out for your police report for your insurance company." They don't wanna be providing such terrible service like that. We need more cops. We need more resources for people to actually get off of drugs, and we need more cops.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: How about affordability? You're talking about property taxes go up, like, 13% over the last year-

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: And what have you gotten for it?

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: And look at all the fees that have gone up, too. And let's look at all the ways that they've tried to pick your pockets, too. I mean, he's saying that he's kept property taxes increases low, but while you're there at the bank standing at the teller paying your property taxes, he's picking your pockets.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: Whether it's making it harder to park in the city and, like, increasing restrictions there and increasing the price and so that they can give out more tickets. I think it was, like, 460,000 tickets last year or something like that. The vacant unit tax. We can look at that, and it's where... You know, there's been a lot of policies at different levels of government in the last decade that have killed the price of-- I mean, the price of houses and the price of rent has skyrocketed.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: The price of building these houses has skyrocketed. The price of maintaining these houses has skyrocketed, but they needed a boogeyman to point at so we didn't look at them, right? So, oh, it's investors buying property and holding it and not renting it out to people. That's why there's an affordability issue, we were told.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: And, you know, in some markets that might be the case, but I don't think it was nearly as big as they'd implied in Ottawa. So now they need something to fight the boogeyman, right? So they come out with the vacant unit tax. And I've had countless calls from senior citizens or from the children of senior citizens saying how badly it's hitting them.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: There's an 82-year-old woman that called me a couple of days ago that was telling me that she lives in a duplex in the Glebe that's been in her family since the '90s. Her husband passed away a couple years ago. So because there's a unit that's technically separate from where she lives in the same house, and she owns it, she's being told by the city that she either has to, at 82, 83 years old, either become a landlord or sell her house, or she's gonna be slapped with, I think, up of 42 to 46,000 next year 'cause it's the third or fourth year that it's been vacant, so it keeps increasing.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: She's telling me that she's on a fixed income. She's on a pension. If this hits her, then she's gonna have to go to a food bank. Or there's another person telling me a story where their mother called and they were like, "I thought I already paid my property taxes. I think I paid it twice."

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: He's like, "Mom, what are you talking about?" So they go to the bank and look at it, and he's like, "Yeah, she paid her property taxes." She doesn't go online. She goes to the bank to pay her bills though. She doesn't go online and see that, oh, I have to report I live in my house that I've lived in for 60 years.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: So they slapped her with a vacant unit tax. She got a bill, she went to the bank, and she paid a bill. So how many people have been paying it without knowing? How many people are put in the position, like the other woman, that now she might have to go to a food bank? Or there's the people whose relative passed away, and now they have to deal with, you know, everything surrounding that, and maybe they need to do some renovations before they can get the unit filled.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: So they go over, and now they're paying a vacant unit tax.

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: So your solution is deregulate-

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: I'm getting rid of the vacant unit tax, 100%. That's gonna be gone. And the policy's going up on the website, and you can see more of the details surrounding that, what it brought in, what we'd be losing, what we're not going to be doing to people anymore.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: But when we talked about affordability, there's a lot more than just keeping property taxes low. That's important. I'm not gonna be saying that I'm going to raise property taxes out the gate. Let's see what kind of savings we can find. I think Mark Sutcliffe said that he's promising to find $250 million in savings in the budget that he wrote.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: So he wrote a budget with a quarter billion dollars worth of fluff in it. I mean, if he can find 250 million, then there's money to be had there, and we can stop just stealing it from people. Look at the three-item limit and how much illegal dumping popped up. So now we've got rural property owners-

segments.speaker: David DiNardo
segments.text: For the garbage.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: For the garbage, yeah. The rural property owners that are having to deal with this dumping on their property. The businesses with a dumpster in the back that they gotta put a lock on now because they're paying to dump it. The construction sites where the bins are full. We go in on a Monday, and the bin's overflowing with household garbage.

segments.speaker: Alex Lawson
segments.text: There's like a couch leaning up against it. I mean, these are the policies that have done this. But I mean, as for, you know, these are some levers that we can pull for affordability. It's not just that property tax line, but let's also... You know, I'm not gonna pretend that I can do something about the price of diesel.
